books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Labor contract, Freedmen’s Bureau records for Mississippi (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47)
Civil Rights Act of March 1, 1875, Section 1, 18 Stat. 335
Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery (1901)
W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources and real data (see each document’s sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the promises of Reconstruction were kept for African Americans between 1865 and 1903.

documents.title: Sharecropping contract: half the crop, after the debts are settled
documents.source: Labor contract, Records of the Field Offices for the State of Mississippi, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, 1865–1872 (National Archives Microfilm M1907, roll 47). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Freedmen’s Bureau labor contract from Mississippi, written between a landowner and freed workers.
documents.text: “…the Parties of the second Part are entitled to receive one half of all crops they may cultivate after a full and entire settlement of all claims the Party of the first Part may have against them arising under this Contract… they further agree that said portion of all crops … shall not be used or removed from the Plantation until all their indebtedness to the Party of the first Part is fully and satisfactorily settled.”

documents.title: Civil Rights Act: equal enjoyment of public places
documents.source: Civil Rights Act of March 1, 1875, Section 1, 18 Stat. 335. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Congress, in its last great Reconstruction law, promising equal access to inns, trains, and theaters.
documents.text: “That all persons within the jurisdiction of the United States shall be entitled to the full and equal enjoyment of the accommodations, advantages, facilities, and privileges of inns, public conveyances on land or water, theaters, and other places of public amusement; subject only to the conditions and limitations established by law, and applicable alike to citizens of every race and color, regardless of any previous condition of servitude.”

documents.title: Reese: the amendment does not confer the vote
documents.source: United States v. Reese, 92 U.S. 214 (1876), majority opinion of Chief Justice Morrison Waite. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Chief Justice Waite, in the first Supreme Court decision on the Fifteenth Amendment.
documents.text: “The Fifteenth Amendment does not confer the right of suffrage upon any one. It prevents the States, or the United States, however, from giving preference, in this particular, to one citizen of the United States over another on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.”

documents.title: Senate report: the flight to Kansas
documents.source: Minority report, Senate Select Committee investigating the Negro Exodus, Senate Report 693, 46th Congress, 2nd Session (1880). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The minority of a Senate committee, reporting on why Black Southerners were fleeing to Kansas.
documents.text: “In the spring of 1879, thousands of colored people, unable longer to endure the intolerable hardships, injustice, and suffering inflicted upon them by a class of Democrats in the South, had, in utter despair, fled panic-stricken from their homes and sought protection among strangers in a strange land. Homeless, penniless, and in rags, these poor people were thronging the wharves of Saint Louis, crowding the steamers on the Mississippi River, and in pitiable destitution throwing themselves upon the charity of Kansas.”

documents.title: Civil Rights Cases: “a mere citizen”
documents.source: Civil Rights Cases, 109 U.S. 3 (1883), majority opinion of Justice Joseph P. Bradley. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Justice Bradley, for an 8–1 Court, striking down the Civil Rights Act of 1875.
documents.text: “When a man has emerged from slavery, and, by the aid of beneficent legislation, has shaken off the inseparable concomitants of that state, there must be some stage in the progress of his elevation when he takes the rank of a mere citizen, and ceases to be the special favorite of the laws, and when his rights as a citizen, or a man, are to be protected in the ordinary modes by which other men’s rights are protected.”

documents.title: Washington remembers the day of freedom
documents.source: Booker T. Washington, Up From Slavery: An Autobiography (1901), Chapter 1. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Booker T. Washington, remembering as an adult the day his family learned they were free.
documents.text: “…some man who seemed to be a stranger (a United States officer, I presume) made a little speech and then read a rather long paper—the Emancipation Proclamation, I think. After the reading we were told that we were all free, and could go when and where we pleased. My mother, who was standing by my side, leaned over and kissed her children, while tears of joy ran down her cheeks. She explained to us what it all meant, that this was the day for which she had been so long praying, but fearing that she would never live to see.”

documents.title: Du Bois: the problem of the color-line
documents.source: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom.” Public domain.
documents.sourcing: W. E. B. Du Bois, opening his chapter on the aftermath of Reconstruction.
documents.text: “The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line,—the relation of the darker to the lighter races of men in Asia and Africa, in America and the islands of the sea. It was a phase of this problem that caused the Civil War; and however much they who marched South and North in 1861 may have fixed on the technical points, of union and local autonomy as a shibboleth, all nevertheless knew, as we know, that the question of Negro slavery was the real cause of the conflict.”

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which Reconstruction failed by 1877, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as emancipation during the Civil War, the Reconstruction Acts, or the debate over who would control Reconstruction.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Panic of 1873, the Mississippi Plan of 1875, the Exodus of 1879, sharecropping, or the Civil Rights Cases of 1883.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of the claim, showing how the same development pulled in opposite directions, or weighing change against continuity.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: the promises of Reconstruction were kept only to a small extent, because freedom and citizenship were written into law but never secured in daily life, though Black institutions and the amendments themselves endured.
Grouping 1 — the economic promise broken: the sharecropping contract (Doc 1) shows freed workers bound by debt instead of given land.
Grouping 2 — the legal promise narrowed: the Civil Rights Act (Doc 2) promises equal public life, but Reese (Doc 3) and the Civil Rights Cases (Doc 5) take the promise apart in the courts.
Grouping 3 — the human answer: the Exodus report (Doc 4) shows families fleeing, while Washington (Doc 6) remembers freedom’s joy and Du Bois (Doc 7) names the color-line that remained.
Outside evidence: the Freedmen’s Bureau schools and Howard and Fisk Universities; the Compromise of 1877; the Mississippi Plan of 1875; Plessy v. Ferguson (1896).
Complexity: the same era that failed to keep its promises still left Black churches, schools, and colleges standing, and the amendments waiting to be enforced again.
